prompt: What does a cold backup (stop the server, copy the directory, start it) cost?
hint: What is the server doing while cp runs?

choices.text: Its consistency, since the files are copied one after another
choices.why: With the server stopped nothing changes during the copy, so every file is from the same moment.

choices.text: The write-ahead log, which a cold copy leaves behind on the server
choices.why: The copy took pg_wal too: 689 of its 991 MB.

choices.text: An outage for as long as the copy takes
choices.why: Right. The copy is perfect, and nobody can use the database while it is taken.

choices.text: Nothing; it is the free version of a base backup
choices.why: It costs the one thing most databases cannot spare: being down.

prompt: The cold copy was 991 MB. How many of those megabytes were the `pg_wal` directory?
hint: The second du.

prompt: Somebody backs up a busy server with `cp -a` of its data directory, and the copy starts without errors. What can be wrong with it?
hint: When was each file copied?

choices.text: Each file is from a different moment
choices.why: Right. Without the log written during the copy, nothing repairs the files into one moment.

choices.text: Nothing: a copy that starts cleanly is consistent
choices.why: It started because crash recovery found nothing it recognised as wrong. That is not the same as consistent.

choices.text: The files belong to the wrong user and the server will refuse them
choices.why: cp -a keeps owners and permissions, and the scenario says it started.

choices.text: Its indexes are missing, because cp skips them
choices.why: cp copies every file; the indexes are there, possibly pointing at rows that are not.

prompt: What would a crash recovery need in order to repair a copy made by `cp` on a running server?
hint: The server already writes it.

choices.text: A list of which files cp copied first
choices.why: The order alone tells recovery nothing about what changed in between.

choices.text: A second copy taken immediately after the first
choices.why: Two inconsistent copies do not make a consistent one.

choices.text: The checksums of every file at the moment the copy started
choices.why: Checksums say whether bytes changed, not what to do about it.

choices.text: All the log written while the copy ran, and a bit before
choices.why: Right. That stretch of write-ahead log is what pg_basebackup collects and backup_label points at.

prompt: Put the steps of `pg_basebackup -X stream -c fast` in the order it reported them.
hint: The log position comes from a checkpoint.
items: Note the write-ahead log start point
Copy the files while a receiver collects the log
Note the end point and write the manifest
trap: The checkpoint fixes the point recovery starts from; the files are copied while the log streams; the end point says how far recovery has to go.

prompt: Why is `-c fast` not the default for `pg_basebackup`?
hint: What does an immediate checkpoint do on a busy server?

choices.text: It skips the checkpoint, which makes the backup unsafe
choices.why: It asks for the checkpoint immediately; it does not skip it.

choices.text: A burst of writes that a busy server feels
choices.why: Right. The default spreads the checkpoint's writes out, and the backup waits for it instead.

choices.text: It only works with -X stream
choices.why: The two are independent; -c chooses the checkpoint, -X the log.

choices.text: It produces a backup without a manifest
choices.why: The manifest is written either way.

prompt: What does `backup_label` tell the server that starts on the copy?
hint: Its first line.

choices.text: Who took the backup, when and why, for the record
choices.why: The LABEL line is a name. What matters to the server is the start location.

choices.text: Where recovery must start in the log
choices.why: Right. The server replays from START WAL LOCATION instead of trusting its control file.

choices.text: Which databases the backup contains
choices.why: A base backup contains all of them; the label does not list databases.

choices.text: The password of the role that took it
choices.why: No password is in it.

prompt: With `-X ___`, `pg_basebackup` collects the write-ahead log over a second connection while the files are copied.
hint: The word for the way a replica receives the log.

prompt: One line of text was appended to `global/pg_control` in the backup. How did `pg_verifybackup` notice?
hint: Look at its error.

choices.text: The server refused to start on the copy
choices.why: pg_verifybackup never starts a server; it reads the files.

choices.text: It read pg_control and found an invalid state
choices.why: It does not interpret the file; it compares it with what the manifest says.

choices.text: The write-ahead log no longer matched the file
choices.why: The error named the file's size, not the log.

choices.text: Its size differed from the manifest's
choices.why: Right. 8201 bytes on disk against 8192 recorded when the server sent it.

prompt: A base backup passes `pg_verifybackup`. What has that established?
hint: Whose bytes are compared with whose?

choices.text: The bytes are what the server sent
choices.why: Right, and the log the copy needs is there too. One class of failure is ruled out; a restore is still the only proof it works.

choices.text: That the database inside is free of corruption
choices.why: A page damaged on the server is copied faithfully and verifies perfectly.

choices.text: That a server will start on it and answer queries
choices.why: Only starting one establishes that.

choices.text: That it matches the live server as it is now
choices.why: It is compared with the manifest written when it was taken, not with the server today.

prompt: Why is `pg_verifybackup` typed as `/usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin/pg_verifybackup`?
hint: Where does Ubuntu put the less common PostgreSQL programs?

choices.text: Because it has to run as root
choices.why: It ran as ana. The full path is about where the program is, not who runs it.

choices.text: Because the name is shared with another program
choices.why: No other program has that name.

choices.text: Ubuntu keeps it out of the PATH
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu wraps the common tools in /usr/bin and leaves the rest in /usr/lib/postgresql/16/bin.

choices.text: Because version 16 renamed it
choices.why: It has had this name since PostgreSQL 13.

prompt: A restore copies the base backup into the data directory and gives it to postgres, but skips `chmod 700`. What happens?
hint: PostgreSQL is particular about who can read its files.

choices.text: The server starts, and anyone on the machine can read the data
choices.why: PostgreSQL checks the directory's permissions at start and refuses rather than run exposed.

choices.text: The server starts read-only until the permissions are fixed
choices.why: There is no such mode; it does not start.

choices.text: Nothing; cp -a already set them
choices.why: The backup was written by ana with ordinary permissions; the restore has to tighten them.

choices.text: The server refuses to start, and says why in its log
choices.why: Right. A data directory readable by others is refused, and the log names the permissions.

prompt: Which log line says the restored copy has become one consistent moment?
hint: Before it, the copy is still being repaired.

choices.text: `database system is ready to accept connections`
choices.why: That comes later, after the checkpoint; consistency was reached before it.

choices.text: `checkpoint starting: end-of-recovery immediate wait`
choices.why: That checkpoint follows recovery; it does not mark consistency.

choices.text: `consistent recovery state reached at 0/2D000100`
choices.why: Right. Replaying up to the backup's end point is what makes the copy consistent.

choices.text: `redo starts at`, the first replay line
choices.why: That is where repair begins, not where it is finished.

prompt: Restoring the base backup needed no `createdb`, no globals file and no roles created first. Why?
hint: Where do roles live on disk?

choices.text: Roles are in the data directory, so the copy carried them
choices.why: Right. The whole server comes back, roles, every database and their owners.

choices.text: pg_basebackup dumps the globals for you
choices.why: It dumps nothing. It copies files, and roles are files like everything else.

choices.text: The restore server already had the same roles from lesson 2
choices.why: Its data directory was deleted and replaced; nothing of it survived.

choices.text: Physical restores skip ownership entirely
choices.why: Ownership is restored exactly as it was, because the catalogue files are copied.

prompt: A storage snapshot of the single volume holding a running server's data directory and log is taken. What state is it in?
hint: As if something had happened at that instant.

choices.text: Inconsistent, like a cp of a running server
choices.why: A cp reads files at different moments; a snapshot captures them all at one.

choices.text: Crash-consistent: as if the power had been cut, which PostgreSQL recovers from
choices.why: Right. Every file is from the same instant, and the log repairs the rest on start.

choices.text: Clean, as if the server had been shut down
choices.why: Nothing flushed or closed; it is the state after a crash, not after a shutdown.

choices.text: Unusable without pg_backup_start
choices.why: A single atomic snapshot is safe without it; the log makes crash recovery work.

prompt: Data and write-ahead log live on two cloud disks. A script snapshots one, then the other, 400 ms later. What is the problem, and the fix?
hint: One crash, or two?

choices.text: None: 400 ms is too short to matter
choices.why: Any writes in those 400 ms make the log describe a history the data copy does not have.

choices.text: The log snapshot is unnecessary; take only the data volume
choices.why: Without the log, crash recovery has nothing to repair the data with.

choices.text: The two are two crashes at two moments; snapshot them as one atomic group
choices.why: Right, or wrap the snapshots in pg_backup_start and pg_backup_stop and keep the label.

choices.text: Run fsfreeze on both volumes and the gap disappears
choices.why: fsfreeze makes each volume clean on its own; it does not make two snapshots one instant.

prompt: Why is a snapshot of your running virtual machine not a backup in this course's sense, although PostgreSQL would recover from it?
hint: Where does the snapshot live?

choices.text: It lives on the computer it protects
choices.why: Right. One failed disk or one deleted machine takes both. Lesson 9 is about that.

choices.text: Because it is not crash-consistent
choices.why: It is: the whole disk is one volume, captured at one instant.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL cannot read a hypervisor's format
choices.why: Restoring the snapshot gives the machine back its disk; PostgreSQL never sees a format.

choices.text: Because it is taken far too often to be useful
choices.why: Frequency is not the issue; location is.

prompt: How many seconds did `pg_basebackup` take for the whole 318 MB server?
hint: The real line.

prompt: Why did the physical restore not slow down with the number of indexes, as lesson 2's logical restore did?
hint: What happened to the indexes in each?

choices.text: The physical restore skipped the indexes and rebuilt them later
choices.why: Nothing is rebuilt later; the indexes arrive as finished files.

choices.text: Base backups compress indexes better than dumps
choices.why: Compression is not the difference. A dump does not contain indexes at all, only the commands to build them.

choices.text: The restore server had more memory for sorting
choices.why: Both restores ran on the same machine.

choices.text: The indexes came back as files, already built
choices.why: Right. Its time depends on the bytes and the disk, not on what has to be rebuilt.

prompt: Which of these can a base backup of a PostgreSQL 16 server NOT do? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about version, scope and damage.

choices.text: Start on PostgreSQL 17
choices.why: Right. A physical copy starts only on the same major version.

choices.text: Restore one table without restoring the server
choices.why: Right. Getting one table back means restoring the whole server somewhere else first.

choices.text: Restore every database on the server at once
choices.why: That is exactly what it does: the whole server comes back.

choices.text: Detect a damaged page that was copied from the server
choices.why: Right. The bytes match the manifest; the damage comes along unremarked.

prompt: A base backup is taken nightly at 02:00. A disk fails at 18:00. How much data is lost?
hint: A base backup is still one moment.

choices.text: Nothing, because a base backup copies the log too
choices.why: It copies the log written during the backup, which ends a minute after 02:00.

choices.text: Sixteen hours, as with a nightly dump
choices.why: Right. Faster to restore, same loss. Lesson 4 keeps the log in between.

choices.text: Only the minutes the backup took
choices.why: Everything after the backup's end point is outside it.

choices.text: Eight hours, half the gap
choices.why: There is no halfway: the backup holds 02:00 and nothing later.

prompt: A team keeps only base backups, verified nightly with `pg_verifybackup`. A bug in a disk controller has been silently damaging pages of one table for a week. What do they find on the day they need a restore?
hint: What does a physical copy do with damage, and what does verification check?

choices.text: A clean copy from before the damage started
choices.why: Only if they still keep a backup older than a week, and nothing in their checks would have told them which one.

choices.text: A week of backups that verify perfectly and carry the damage
choices.why: Right. A dump would have failed on the bad pages; keeping both kinds is how a failure shows up in one of them.

choices.text: The verification failing every night for a week, unnoticed
choices.why: Verification compares the copy with what the server sent, which matched. It passed every night.

choices.text: A restore that refuses to start
choices.why: A damaged table page does not stop a server starting; it surfaces when the table is read.
